summary: A method for converting Network Graphics Protocol Level 0 coordinates to device-specific integer coordinates. RFC 387 had discussed converting them to floating point, but real devices need integer addresses. The note shows how to map to integers from zero to the device's maximum screen address.

eli5.summary: A way to turn the position numbers in the drawing rules into the exact whole-number spots on a real screen.

questions: convert graphics coordinates to device coordinates
how to convert ngp coordinates to device coordinates
why use integer instead of floating point coordinates
subtitle: How to turn Network Graphics Protocol coordinates into whole-number screen positions with a shift, a multiply and an add.

tldr.problem: Real display devices need integer addresses, but converting NGP-0 coordinates to floating point (as discussed in RFC 387) is slow and awkward.
tldr.mechanism: Treat the coordinate as a two's complement fraction, sign-extend it, multiply by an odd integer Q if needed, shift by (I-n) and add the offset S.
tldr.outcome: The integer procedure is generally much faster than the floating point one. The note updates RFC 387 and is listed with status Unknown.

today: RFC 401 updates RFC 387 and is marked with status Unknown in the metadata. It has not been obsoleted by any later RFC.

sections.title: The Conversion Problem
sections.content:
RFC 387 discussed converting NGP-0 coordinates to floating point PDP-10 coordinates. This note observes that this is generally undesirable, because real devices require integer addressing.

It therefore describes a way to convert NGP coordinates to integer coordinates in the range zero to M, where M is the maximum address of the device screen, on a machine using 2's complement arithmetic. The author says the algorithm could be modified for one's complement or sign-magnitude machines.
sections.eli5: Screens count in whole steps, not fractions. This note shows how to get whole steps from the fractions the drawing rules use.

sections.title: The NGP Coordinate Format
sections.content:
An NGP coordinate puts a sign in the most significant bit, followed by n bits of fractional information. The initial implementation of NGP requires N=15. Negative numbers are represented in 2's complement.

Conversion to a device coordinate is D = S * f + S, where D is the integer device coordinate, S is a scaling factor (typically M/2) and f is the NGP fractional coordinate.
sections.eli5: A position is a fraction between minus one and one. Multiply by half the screen size and add the middle, and you land on a screen spot.

sections.title: The Integer Procedure
sections.content:
The note writes S = Q * 2^I, where Q is an odd integer and I is an integer. The expression becomes D = Q * 2^(I-n) * (2^n * f) + S.

The factor 2^n * f is obtained simply by extending the sign bit into the upper part of the word. If Q is 1, as with many devices, the multiply can be ignored. The 2^(I-n) factor is an arithmetic shift left by (I-n), or right by (n-I). The offset S is then added with an integer add.

  1. Move the coordinate to a register and extend the sign.
  2. Integer multiply by Q (if necessary).
  3. Arithmetic shift left by (I-n).
  4. Integer add S.
sections.eli5: Instead of doing fraction math, you slide the digits over and add a number. Sliding digits is much quicker for a computer.

sections.title: Why It Is Faster
sections.content:
The alternative is to move the coordinate to a register, float it, do a floating point multiply and add, and convert back to fixed point. The note says the integer procedure would generally be much faster.

On most machines an integer multiply is faster than a floating point multiply. On a PDP-10 the multiply can usually be done with no access to memory, since Q is usually small.
sections.eli5: Four quick steps beat five slow ones, so the screen can be drawn sooner.
